title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated identification system that was acted on as if it were confirmed fact. A license-plate reader misread a single character and produced a match to a stolen vehicle, and the alert was treated as sufficient grounds for an armed stop rather than as a lead to be checked. The failure sits at the handoff between the system's output and the officer's decision, which is the point where a machine's guess becomes a real-world enforcement action.

The vendor's own position, that alerts should be independently verified before enforcement, describes the check that did not happen. Catching this would have required confirming the plate against the vehicle in front of the deputy, or confirming the hit through a second source, before the stop escalated. A single misread character is the kind of error these systems are known to produce, which is why the verification step exists.

What is not established is whether the deputy's conduct was lawful or whether the tinted plate cover the sheriff's office blames was in fact the cause, since that explanation comes from the agency defending the stop and not from an independent finding. The account rests on a single outlet's reporting.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, a 42-year-old motorist in York County, South Carolina, was reportedly held at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
title_en: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover
